newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: BASF hope to seal $1 bln Malaysian venture soon.
newsitem.headline: BASF hope to seal $1 bln Malaysian venture soon.

text.p: German chemical giant, BASF AG hopes to sign a letter of intent soon with Malaysian state-owned Petroliam Nasional Bhd to build a US$ 1.0 billion petrochemical complex, a senior BASF official said on Monday.

"We signed a letter of understanding (with Petronas) and are confident in a few months of signing a letter of intent and have project details," Volker Trautz, a member of the BASF board of executive directors told reporters at the sidelines of the second Asia-Pacific Chemical Industry meeting.
Trautz said he was optimistic that within the next three to four months the company would iron out the details for the project with Petronas.
Earlier this month, Petronas said the two companies would build the complex in the eastern state of Pahang in peninsular Malaysia and it would start production in 2001.
The three new plants the two companies intend to build are an oxo alcohol plant with an annual capacity of 250,000 tonnes, a 100,000 tonne plasticiser unit and a 40,000 tonne phthalic anhydride unit.
To secure the feedstock supplies to these plants, Petronas and BASF plan to build a 275,000-300,000 tonne per year propane dehydrogenation unit.
The final plasticiser products to be produced at the complex are used to strengthen plastic products.
When signed, the agreement will expand the cooperation arrangement between the two companies to build other plants at the same location.
Last April, BASF and Petronas signed a letter of intent to build an acrylic plant at a cost of US$250 million. The plant, with an annual capacity of 160,000 tonnes, will be ready by the end of 1999.
Acrylic monomers are used in the production of paints and coatings as well as hygiene products like nappies.
Trautz said BASF was also going ahead with a plan to build a 6 billion mark (U.S.$3.6 billion) petrochemical complex in China that includes a naphtha cracker, styrene and polystyrene plants.
Despite projected overcapacity in Asia, Trautz said the company's strategy of teaming up with strong local partners enhanced the competitiveness of the projects.

"In Malaysia, for example, we will join forces with Petronas, combining Petronas' strength in feedstock with our strength in technology, establishing a joint venture that wull hold a cost leadership position," he said.
